:::{#thm-gram-properties}
#### Entries and symmetry of a Gram matrix

Let $\matr{A}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with columns $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_n$,
and let $\matr{G} = \tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}$ (@def-gram-matrix).

1. Entry $(i, j)$ of $\matr{G}$ is $\vecf{a}_i \cdot \vecf{a}_j$.
2. $\matr{G}$ is symmetric (@def-symmetric-matrix).
3. $\qform{\matr{G}}{\vx} = \norm{\matr{A} \vx}^2 \ge 0$ for every $\vx \in \reals^n$,
   so $\matr{G}$ is [positive semidefinite](linear-algebra.qmd#def-positive-semidefinite).

:::

::: proof

**Entries.**
Row $i$ of $\tp{\matr{A}}$ is $\tp{\vecf{a}_i}$,
so entry $(i, j)$ of $\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}$ is the dot product of that row with column $j$ of $\matr{A}$,
namely $\tp{\vecf{a}_i} \vecf{a}_j = \vecf{a}_i \cdot \vecf{a}_j$.

**Symmetry.**
The dot product is commutative, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{ij} &= \vecf{a}_i \cdot \vecf{a}_j \\
&= \vecf{a}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i \\
&= g_{ji}.
\end{aligned}
$$

**Positive semidefiniteness.**
For any $\vx$,

$$
\ba
\qform{\matr{G}}{\vx}
&= \tp{\vx}\,\tp{\matr{A}}\,\matr{A} \vx
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{G} \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{A} \vx)}\,(\matr{A} \vx)
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \norm{\matr{A} \vx}^2
&& \text{(@eq-l2-norm, squared)}
\\
&\ge 0.
&& \text{(a squared norm is nonnegative)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-gram-properties}
#### Checking the properties on a small Gram matrix

For $\matr{A}$ in @exm-gram-matrix, $\matr{G} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
It is symmetric: $g_{12} = g_{21} = 1$.
Take $\vx = (1, -1)$. Then

$$
\ba
\qform{\matr{G}}{\vx}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(} \matr{G} \vx = (1, -1) \text{)}
\\
&= 2,
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\ea
$$

and $\matr{A} \vx = (1, 0, -1)$ has $\norm{\matr{A} \vx}^2 = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2$,
as the theorem says.
The converse (every positive semidefinite matrix is a Gram matrix) is
[this theorem](linear-algebra.qmd#thm-pd-gram).

:::
